newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB profit transfer to Swiss govts leaps.
newsitem.headline: SNB profit transfer to Swiss govts leaps.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) said it will transfer roughly one billion Swiss francs to the Swiss federal government and cantons from 1996 earnings, up from 142 million on 1995 profits.
Its total net surplus for 1996 was equal to 7.6 billion Swiss francs.
"The remainder of the amount (of 7.6 billion) will serve to ensure a continual profit payout in subsequent years," the SNB said in its annual report.

The transfer includes 600 million francs as a regular payment and an additional 458 million for 1995, bringing the amount for 1995 up to 600 million as well, including the 142 million transfer last year.

The SNB said the increase resulted from gains in the value of other currencies versus the Swiss franc and extraordinary earnings due to revisions in accounting which included revaluing some assets, excluding gold.
Gold is still set at the legal parity of 4,595.74 Swiss francs per kilo, based on a parliamentary decision from 1971.

The SNB intends to revalue gold at around 60 percent of market prices if parliament and voters approve a plan to create a Swiss Solidarity Foundation to benefit victims of poverty, catastrophes and human rights abuses, including the Holocaust.
This could free up seven billion francs in gold for the fund, and an additional seven billion francs for other purposes.

The SNB said that a one-time revaluation of its currency holdings, domestic money market claims, domestic securities, and open forward positions in currencies and securities resulted in an extraordinary gain of 1.5 billion francs.

The revaluing of holdings and assets also led to a release of reserves totaling 500 million francs. A revaluation of foreign currency reserves to year-end levels versus mid-December levels led to a book gain of around 700 million Swiss francs.

The SNB said that its gross profits actually fell in 1996 versus the previous year to 2.18 billion francs from 2.29 billion. But the franc's depreciation led to an increase in the foreign currency post by 4.4 billion francs versus a decline of 3.5 billion in 1995.
"Together with the one-time gains and book profits from the changes in accounting, the total profits were roughly 8.5 billion francs. The aimed-for provisions rose by 900 million," the SNB said.
